papers.not_read: The text layer lost the values after the arrows for depth and two-qubit gates on the Application Specific Compilation slide (PDF p.29), scrambled the cell order of the GWAS table (PDF p.13) and of the hepatitis B counts (PDF p.14), and does not carry the images: example generated molecules (p.7), the decision trees (p.11), the flight path map (p.18), the binomial tree (p.28), the ansatz circuit drawings (p.32), the VQE results plots (p.33) and the VITE plots (p.34). All other text on the 35 pages was read.
papers.what_it_is: A confidential vendor slide deck from Bleximo's Head of Quantum Engineering that surveys candidate quantum computing applications in drug design, genetics, flight routing, fertilizer chemistry, derivative pricing and molecular simulation.

assertions.value: The document is a slide deck titled "An Overview of Bleximo’s Applications", presented by Fabio Sanches, Head of Quantum Engineering at Bleximo, and marked "Confidential and Proprietary".
assertions.anchor: Title slide, PDF p.1
quotes: An Overview of Bleximo’s Applications
Fabio Sanches Head of Quantum Engineering fabio@bleximo.com
Confidential and Proprietary
assertions.certainty_reason: The title slide states the authorship, the vendor and the confidentiality marking.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a vendor overview deck of slides. It gives no methods sections, no baselines and no error bars, so every result in it is a vendor statement that cannot be reproduced from the deck alone.

assertions.value: The paper describes a variational autoencoder as encoding an input x into a low dimensional latent space representation and decoding the latent vector into an output that is as similar as possible to x, and a Grammar VAE as imposing a grammar so that discrete data such as molecular structures can be smoothly encoded into and generated from the model. The slide cites arXiv:1703.01925.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Grammar Variational Autoencoder", PDF p.4
quotes: The goal of VAE is to encode input x into a low dimensional latent space representation
Grammar VAE model impose a grammar such that discrete data such as molecular structures can be smoothly encoded into and generated from the model
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of a model from cited work (arXiv:1703.01925), not a result of this deck.

assertions.value: On the ZINC dataset the slide states that the model can encode and decode same or similar molecules and provide good property prediction, and shows for one molecule the properties logD, qed and SAS: predicted [2.839, 0.799, 2.331] against correct [2.391, 0.630, 2.200].
assertions.anchor: Slide "Molecule Generation and Prediction Results (ZINC Dataset)", PDF p.5
quotes: The model can encode and decode same/similar molecules and provide good property prediction
Properties: [ logD, qed , SAS ] Predicted: [2.839, 0.799, 2.331] Correct: [2.391, 0.630, 2.200]
assertions.certainty_reason: One example molecule on one slide. The slide gives no error metric over a test set and does not say whether the run is the deck author's or the cited paper's.
assertions.reader_inference: For this molecule the predicted values differ from the correct ones by 0.448, 0.169 and 0.131 respectively. One example does not show the quality of the prediction in general, and the slide does not call the 0.448 gap in logD good or bad.

assertions.value: The authors state that by slightly perturbing latent vectors the model can generate similarly structured molecules with slightly different properties, and that this gives the possibility of optimizing drug properties. The slide gives one SMILES string as an example.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Perturbation of Latent Space", PDF p.6
quotes: By slightly perturbing latent vectors, the model can generate similar structured molecules with slightly different properties.
This gives the possibility of optimizing drug properties.
SMILES: COc1cc(C=N)ccc1OC(=O)c1c(C)noc1C
assertions.reader_inference: No measured optimization of a property is given in the text layer; the example molecules are images (PDF p.7).

assertions.value: The slide states that current algorithms already show advantages for quantum machine learning in processing quantum data, attributing this to Google, and states promising prospects for incorporating quantum generative modeling for synthesizing molecules with better property prediction, since molecules are quantum systems.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Quantum Generative Models for Drug synthesis", PDF p.8
quotes: Current algorithms already show that there are advantages for Quantum Machine Learning in processing quantum data (Google).
Promising prospects for incorporating quantum generative modeling for synthesizing molecules with better property prediction, since these are quantum systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An outlook statement and an attribution to Google with no reference, no numbers and no experiment in the deck.
assertions.reader_inference: The deck shows no quantum generative model result; the only quantum machine learning content on this slide is the unreferenced attribution to Google.

assertions.value: The paper describes the UK Biobank as 500k volunteers in the UK with 15,280 facts about each patient, whole exome sequencing complete in July of 2022 (30 million nucleotides), and genotyping with more than 805,426 single nucleotide polymorphisms tracked across the participants. It describes Explorys as a US hospital database holding every diagnosis and treatment for 64 million patients.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Medical databases and biobanks", PDF p.10
quotes: UK Biobank [broad set of features]
500k volunteers in the UK
15,280 facts about each patient
Whole exome sequencing complete in July of 2022 (30 million nucleotides)
Genotyping with > 805,426 total single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) tracked across the participants.
Medical database collected in U.S. from hospitals
64 million patients
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide sets out the datasets the genetics and medicine analyses draw on.
assertions.reader_inference: The deck gives no source for these dataset figures; they are the data description, not a result.

assertions.value: The slide titled "Decision trees to predict fatality from COVID-19" shows trees whose predicates are inequalities on continuous variables, set membership and binaries, and states that boosting aims to combine these trees, each a weak predictor, into a strong predictor, and that dominant effects change depending on bootstrapping.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Decision trees to predict fatality from COVID-19", PDF p.11
quotes: Decision trees to predict fatality from COVID-19
Predicates involving inequalities on continuous variables.
Boosting aims to combine these trees, each weak predictors, into a strong predictor.
Dominant effects change depending on bootstrapping.
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide shows a method and a qualitative observation. It gives no accuracy, no sample size and no test split.
assertions.reader_inference: The deck gives no performance figure for the trees or the boosted model, so no accuracy claim can be taken from it.

assertions.value: The authors list ranked features for the COVID-19 model under the heading "Coping with undesired correlated features". In the unrestricted ranking the first feature is Age, the second is green space in buffer and the third is waist circumference.
assertions.anchor: Slide "COVID-19 risk factor details", PDF p.12
quotes: Coping with undesired correlated features
Rank Feature 1: f_34_0_0, Age 2: f_24503_0_0, Green space in buffer 3: f_48_0_0, Waist circumference
assertions.certainty_reason: One ranking from one run; the slide gives no importance scores, no stability measure and no definition of the ranking method.
assertions.reader_inference: Green space in buffer and domestic garden percent are environmental variables likely to correlate with location, which seems to be why the authors prohibit some fields in the next ranking.

assertions.value: After some fields are prohibited, the slide shows two bootstrap rankings of features. Age is first in both; waist circumference and particulate matter air pollution take the second and third places, in opposite orders in the two rankings, so the lower ranks change between bootstraps.
assertions.anchor: Slide "COVID-19 risk factor details", PDF p.12 (the text layer interleaves the two lists)
quotes: Rank Feature (prohibiting some fields) 1: f_34_0_0, Age
2: f_48_0_0, Waist circumference
3: f_24005_0_0, Particulate matter air pollution (pm10 um)
2: f_24005_0_0, Particulate matter air pollution (pm10 um)
3: f_48_0_0, Waist circumference
assertions.certainty_reason: Two bootstrap rankings with no scores; the text layer scrambles which list belongs to which bootstrap.
assertions.reader_inference: The reordering of ranks 2 and 3 between bootstraps agrees with the slide on p.11 that dominant effects change depending on bootstrapping.

assertions.value: The slide titled "Genome Wide Associations (individual)" tabulates seven single nucleotide polymorphisms by SNP, chromosome, N and p-value with multiple test correction. The seven rs identifiers are rs139952490, rs3775992, rs148658153, rs117904287, rs6714314, rs112150364 and rs116587930.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Genome Wide Associations (individual)", PDF p.13. The corrected p-values printed in the layer are 0.245, 0.64, 0.77, 0.985, 0.99, 0.99 and 1, but the cell order is scrambled.
quotes: Genome Wide Associations (individual)
p-value (with multiple test correction)
assertions.certainty_reason: A table whose cells the text layer scrambled; the pairing of SNP, chromosome, N and p-value cannot be rebuilt from the layer.
assertions.reader_inference: Every corrected p-value printed in the layer is 0.245 or higher, so none of the seven SNPs is significant on the slide's own correction. This is the reader's reading of the layer; the slide draws no conclusion in text.

assertions.value: The authors state that in 1998 some research caused concern that hepatitis B vaccination might be linked with multiple sclerosis, that this has been debunked by multiple studies, and ask whether other immunizations could be examined and whether these databases could address fear of COVID-19 vaccines.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Multiple sclerosis and immunizations (Explorys)", PDF p.14
quotes: In 1998, some research caused concern that hepatitis B vaccination might be linked with multiple sclerosis (MS).
This has been debunked by multiple studies.
What about other immunizations? Could these databases be used to address fear of COVID-19 vaccines?
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide states the question the Explorys analysis addresses.

assertions.value: The authors report odds ratios from 2x2 tables on Explorys data for several vaccines: varicella virus live 0.05403197 (p-value < 2.2e-16), diphtheria toxoid vaccine 0.7397352 (p-value = 1.781e-09), meningococcal polysaccharide 0.03481072 (p-value < 2.2e-16), Streptococcus pneumoniae 2.967898 (p-value < 2.2e-16), hepatitis A 0.123281 (p-value < 2.2e-16) and hepatitis B 0.1454459 (p-value < 2.2e-16).
assertions.anchor: Slide "Multiple sclerosis and immunizations (Explorys)", PDF p.14. The text layer does not label the rows and columns of the 2x2 tables.
quotes: Varicella virus live FALSE TRUE
p-value < 2.2e-16 odds ratio 0.05403197
p-value = 1.781e-09 odds ratio 0.7397352
p-value < 2.2e-16 odds ratio 0.03481072
p-value < 2.2e-16 odds ratio 2.967898
p-value < 2.2e-16 odds ratio 0.123281
p-value < 2.2e-16 odds ratio 0.1454459
assertions.certainty_reason: A single-database analysis on a slide, without a stated outcome definition, covariate adjustment or multiple-test correction.
assertions.reader_inference: Five of the six odds ratios are below 1 and Streptococcus pneumoniae is above 1. The layer does not say which table axis is vaccination and which is multiple sclerosis, so the direction of each odds ratio cannot be fixed from the text. The slide draws no conclusion in text. Strong unadjusted associations of this kind in a records database can reflect who is vaccinated and who is diagnosed rather than an effect of the vaccine.

assertions.value: The slide shows an "Overall" table with the counts 11408, 580, 4520 and 960.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Multiple sclerosis and immunizations (Explorys)", PDF p.14
quotes: FALSE TRUE FALSE 11408 580 TRUE 4520 960
assertions.certainty_reason: Counts only; the layer does not label the axes and the slide gives no odds ratio for this table.
assertions.reader_inference: The four counts sum to 17468 records, which is the same total as each of the other tables whose counts are readable; the overall table therefore seems to describe the same cohort.

assertions.value: The authors state that the combinatorics of high dimensional biological systems are often classically intractable, ask how treatments and health history interact to predict outcomes, and say that promising quantum algorithms now exist, citing QBoost (arXiv:0912.0779) and IPBoost (arXiv:2002.04679).
assertions.anchor: Slide "Quantum computing helps to decode biological complexity", PDF p.15
quotes: Combinatorics of high dimensional biological systems are often classically intractable.
Promising quantum algorithms now exist: QBoost: arXiv:0912.0779 IPBoost: arXiv:2002.04679
assertions.certainty_reason: An unevidenced claim of intractability and a pointer to two cited algorithms; the deck runs neither.
assertions.reader_inference: No quantum computation is run on the genetics data anywhere in the deck. The classical decision-tree and boosting results on p.11 to p.14 are not tied to a quantum speedup by any measurement.

assertions.value: The authors state that CO2 emissions suggest picking routes that minimize fuel burn (roughly the shortest path), that other contributions and regulations make the climate contribution a more complicated optimization problem, and that a simple shortest path is not the most climate-friendly trajectory.
assertions.anchor: Slides "Optimizing airplane trajectories for climate impact" and "A simple example", PDF p.17 and p.18
quotes: The climate contribution from CO2 emissions suggest we should pick routes that minimize fuel burn (roughly shortest path).
However, other contributions, along with regulations transforms the climate contribution into a more complicated optimization problem.
Simple shortest path is not the most climate-friendly trajectory!
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated as the motivation, with a two-path picture whose details are in an image.

assertions.value: The authors report that Bleximo's solution gave a 24% reduction in flight contribution to global temperature rise for a sample of 100 flights across Europe, compared with the shortest path, with a 1 second runtime.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Bleximo’s Solution", PDF p.19
quotes: 24% reduction in flight contribution to global temperature rise for sample 100 flights across Europe, as compared to shortest path.
1 second runtime.
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's own result on one sample, with no method, no baseline detail, no climate model named and no variance.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide does not say whether the solver is classical or quantum, which climate metric is used, or how the 100 flights were chosen. It gives no hardware, so the result cannot be read as evidence for quantum advantage.

assertions.value: The authors state that additional constraints such as flight interaction can be considered to improve solution quality while satisfying regulations, and that mature quantum computing architectures can be designed to target such optimization problems.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Improvements from Quantum Computing", PDF p.20
quotes: Additional constraints such as flight interaction can be considered to improve solution quality while satisfying regulations.
Mature quantum computing architectures can be designed to target such optimization problems
assertions.certainty_reason: A forward-looking vendor statement with no experiment.

assertions.value: The slide states that ammonia is currently produced through the Haber-Bosch process, responsible for 2% of total energy consumption, and that nitrogenase can be used to convert nitrogen gas and protons to ammonia.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Climate Impact from Fertilizer Production", PDF p.22
quotes: Ammonia is currently produced through the Haber-Bosch process, responsible for 2% of total energy consumption.
Nitrogenase can be used to convert Nitrogen gas and protons to Amonia
assertions.certainty_reason: A background figure with no reference on the slide.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide gives no scope for the 2% figure (world or a country, energy or electricity).

assertions.value: The authors state that the FeMoco protein is a key component in the active site of nitrogenase, responsible for the reaction, and that the details of how this reaction occurs are not known.
assertions.anchor: Slide "An Important Part of Nitrogenase", PDF p.23
quotes: The FeMoco protein is a key component in the active site of nitrogenase, responsible for the reaction.
The details for how this reaction occurs is not known.
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide states the open scientific question that motivates the simulation.
assertions.reader_inference: FeMoco is an iron-molybdenum cofactor, which is generally described as a cofactor rather than a protein; the slide's wording "protein" is the authors' own.

assertions.value: The authors state that accurate simulation of the nitrogenase reaction will require error-corrected quantum computers, that resource estimates using existing codes and algorithms still result in a days-to-months timescale for the simulation, and that application specific devices will reduce simulation overheads.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Application Specific Devices will Reduce Simulation Overheads", PDF p.24
quotes: Application Specific Devices will Reduce Simulation Overheads
Accurate simulation of the reaction will require errorcorrected quantum computers.
Resource estimates using existing codes and algorithms still result in days-months timescale for the simulation.
assertions.certainty_reason: The resource estimate has no reference and no number of qubits or gates; the claim that application specific devices reduce overhead has no figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide gives no source for the days-to-months estimate and no estimate for an application specific device, so the stated reduction of overhead is not quantified.

assertions.value: The slide states a provable, theoretical quadratic speed-up for estimating the expected value of a random variable, and attributes it to Montanaro, "Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods."
assertions.anchor: Slide "Derivative Pricing", PDF p.26
quotes: Quantum speedup for Monte Carlo Provable, theoretical quadratic speed-up for estimating the expected value of a random variable
Montanaro, “Quantum speedup of Monte Carlo methods.”
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to other work; the statement and its conditions are not quoted in this deck.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide gives no conditions of the speedup (for example the access model for the random variable). The speedup is in the number of samples or queries, not in wall-clock time.

assertions.value: The slide states that the speed-up in practice will depend on how the operations are expressed in terms of native operations that real hardware can actually perform, and cites Rebentrost et al., "Quantum computational finance: Monte Carlo pricing of financial derivatives."
assertions.anchor: Slide "Quantum computing for Monte Carlo – from theory to reality", PDF p.27
quotes: Speed-up in practice will depend on how these operations are expressed in terms of native operations that real hardware can actually perform
Rebentrost et. al. "Quantum computational finance: Monte Carlo pricing of financial derivatives."
assertions.certainty_reason: A qualification of the theoretical speedup, with a citation and no figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide itself states that the theoretical quadratic speedup need not carry over to real hardware.

assertions.value: For a single-period binomial tree option pricing circuit, the authors compare generic compilation with Bleximo's application-specific compilation. The slide gives a depth of 18 and a count of 10 two-qubit gates, each followed by an arrow to a value that the text layer lost.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Application Specific Compilation", PDF p.29 and the following depth and gate lines (page text on p.29). The values after the arrows are not in the text layer.
quotes: Quantum algorithm for Monte Carlo requires implementing payoff circuit.
Generic Compilation:
= Bleximo’s application-specific compilation
Two qubit gates: 10 →
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor comparison whose result values are missing from the text layer.
assertions.reader_inference: The arrows suggest that depth 18 and 10 two-qubit gates are the generic-compilation values and that the application-specific values are smaller. The layer does not say so and does not give the new values, so this is the reader's reading of the slide.

assertions.value: The authors state that standard transformations of molecular Hamiltonians result in many unphysical states, and that restricting to physical states with correct occupation numbers and symmetries dramatically reduces qubit requirements. They report qubit counts for HCl, HBr, F2, Cl2 and Br2 of 16, 32, 16, 16 and 16 with the Jordan-Wigner encoding and 6, 8, 6, 6 and 6 with the qubit-efficient encoding.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Efficient Qubit Encoding", PDF p.31
quotes: Standard transformations results in many unphysical states
Restricting to physical states (with correct occupation numbers and symmetries) dramatically reduces qubit requirements.
HCl HBr F2 Cl2 Br2
Jordan-Wigner Qubit Count 16 32 16 16 16
Qubit-Efficient Encoding Qubit Count 6 8 6 6 6
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor table of qubit counts for five small molecules; the encoding is not described on the slide.
assertions.reader_inference: The counts are a resource count, not an accuracy result. The slide does not say what basis set or active space was used, so the counts cannot be reproduced from the deck.

assertions.value: The authors describe an ansatz circuit built from layers of Ry-entangling blocks and Rx-entangling blocks: 8 layers of each, with 56 CNOT gates and 224 parameters, and a smaller variant with 2 layers of each.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Construction of Ansatz Circuit", PDF p.32
quotes: 8 layers of Ry-entangling blocks + 8 layers of Rxentangling blocks
56 CNOT gates and 224 Parameters
2 layers of Ry-entangling blocks + 2 layers of Rx-entangling blocks
assertions.certainty_reason: The slide states the circuit construction used for the VQE runs.
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer does not say which molecule or which qubit count the 56 CNOT gates and 224 parameters refer to, nor which of the two layer counts they belong to.

assertions.value: The slide titled "Chemistry and Quantum Simulation" states the aim of improving accuracies in molecular models, for example for drug discovery, using variants of the Variational Quantum Eigensolver tuned for specific classes of molecules. The slide titled "VQE Results" holds no text beyond its title in the text layer.
assertions.anchor: Slides "Chemistry and Quantum Simulation" and "VQE Results", PDF p.30 and p.33
quotes: Improving accuracies in molecular models, e.g., for drug discovery
Variants of the Variational Quantum Eigensolver, tuned for specific classes of molecules
VQE Results
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement of aim; the VQE results themselves are in a figure that the text layer does not carry.
assertions.reader_inference: No energy, error or convergence figure for the VQE runs is available from the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that for the water molecule, variational imaginary time evolution (VITE) converges to chemical accuracy 100X faster than VQE (QEE, 8 qubits) using 1 extra qubit, for a total of 9 qubits for VITE.
assertions.anchor: Slide "Variational Imaginary Time Evolution (VITE)", PDF p.34
quotes: For water molecule, VITE converges to chemical accuracy 100X faster than VQE (QEE, 8 qubits) using 1 extra qubit (total 9 qubits for VITE)
assertions.certainty_reason: A vendor's own result on one molecule; the slide does not say how faster is measured (iterations, time or circuit evaluations) and the supporting plot is an image.
assertions.reader_inference: The slide names one molecule and one comparison. It does not show that the speedup holds for other molecules or on hardware.
